summary: Gives advice on when it is safe to begin sending data on a label switched path set up with RSVP-TE. Each node is programmed as signaling messages are processed, so data sent too early can be lost or misdelivered. It is informational.

eli5.summary: You should wait until a road is fully built before driving on it. This explains how to know that an MPLS path is ready before sending traffic.

subtitle: When to start sending data on a routed path being established

tldr.problem: When a network router establishes a path through multiple switches to carry data, each switch needs to be programmed to forward packets correctly. Data sent before all switches are ready gets lost or misdirected.
tldr.mechanism: RSVP-TE uses signaling messages to set up these paths node by node. This RFC clarifies when each node is programmed and when endpoints can safely start sending.
tldr.outcome: Networks can safely pipeline the setup process, starting to forward data earlier without risking misdelivery. The guidance also helps performance measurements distinguish setup time from message propagation delays.

facts.label: Safety concern
facts.value: Optical laser activation without ready paths

today: RFC 6383 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It clarifies existing RSVP-TE procedures and is widely referenced in implementations and performance benchmarking standards.

sections.title: The Cross-Connect Problem
sections.content:
Label Switched Paths (LSPs) in MPLS and GMPLS networks are established using RSVP-TE signaling. Signaling messages travel from ingress to egress, and each router along the path configures its forwarding rules (called cross-connects) as messages are processed. These cross-connects tell the router which incoming traffic to send where.

The core problem: data sent before all cross-connects are in place gets lost or sent the wrong way. In optical networks, there is also a physical safety concern: lasers must not be turned on until the path is complete, or service personnel could be hurt.
sections.eli5: Each router gets a message telling it how to forward traffic on this path. If a router hasn't been told yet, it does not know where to send the traffic.

sections.title: Unidirectional LSPs in MPLS-TE
sections.content:
RFC 3209 describes MPLS-TE using one-way paths. Each router waits to receive a Path message from upstream, programs its cross-connect, then sends a Resv message back upstream. The RFC says a router should be prepared to forward packets carrying the assigned label prior to sending the Resv message. This means the cross-connect must be in place before the Resv is sent, not after. Upstream routers can assume that the downstream router is ready to receive traffic once the Resv arrives.

The ingress (starting point) must do two things before sending data: it must receive a Resv message from the egress, and it must program its own cross-connect. Only then is the bidirectional flow of control messages complete.
sections.eli5: Each router tells the one before it, 'I am ready to forward traffic.' The first router can start sending once the last router sends that message back.

sections.title: GMPLS and Suggested Labels
sections.content:
GMPLS extends RSVP-TE to other switching technologies (optical, TDM, Ethernet). It introduces the Suggested_Label object, which lets an upstream router tell a downstream router which label to use. This enables pipelining: the upstream router can start programming its cross-connect for that label before receiving confirmation that the downstream router accepted it.

The trade-off is risk: if the downstream router rejects the label and the upstream router has already programmed, the path fails. The upstream router must include a mechanism to report failure (using PathErr messages) if the cross-connect programming fails to complete before the Resv arrives.
sections.eli5: A router can guess which label will be used and start setting up in the background, saving time. But if the guess is wrong, it must quickly say so.

sections.title: Bidirectional LSPs
sections.content:
Bidirectional paths in GMPLS carry traffic in both directions using a single signaling exchange: Path messages from ingress to egress, Resv from egress to ingress. Each direction has separate forwarding state.

Forward direction (ingress to egress): follows the unidirectional rules in Section 3.1 of RFC 3209. The ingress waits for the Resv message before sending data.

Reverse direction (egress to ingress): uses the Upstream_Label object in the Path message. This label is announced by the upstream (ingress) router before receiving the Resv. RFC 3473 requires this label to be 'valid for forwarding at the time the Path message is sent.' This means the egress can safely send traffic upstream as soon as it processes the Path message, before sending the Resv back. No waiting for the Resv is needed.
sections.eli5: For the reverse path, the sending router prepares a label before getting confirmation, and the receiving router can use it immediately. This saves time in both directions.

sections.title: Testing and Administrative Safety
sections.content:
GMPLS offers an Admin_Status object to put an LSP in 'Administratively Down' state. The LSP exists (all cross-connects are in place), but no traffic flows. Lasers are off in optical systems. This state allows testing of connectivity without risking the delivery of user data.

For example, in an optical network, a connection verification test can run to confirm the path works. In packet networks, a Virtual Circuit Connectivity Verification (VCCV) exchange can check the path. Once testing passes, the LSP is moved to active and user traffic can begin.

This is especially valuable when the control-plane processor is physically separate from the data-plane switch, where control-plane signaling completion does not guarantee data-plane programming success.
sections.eli5: Before turning on lasers or sending real traffic, administrators can test that the path actually works. If something is wrong, they find out before any user data is lost.
